slide_text: Inventing Neural Networks In the Gradient Descent chapter you taught a computer to fit a line: pick weights, measure the error, nudge every weight downhill, repeat. That one loop is more powerful than it looks — the only thing standing between you and a neural network is the shape of the function you feed it. In this chapter you will: Turn a line into a yes/no classifier — and discover what the field calls it. Trip over the most classic training bug and fix it. Chain small functions together and watch weights reshape curves. Take on a problem no straight line can solve — a realistic income-tax rule — and beat it three ways, ending with the activation function that powers modern deep learning. You need , , and your gradient-descent instincts from Chapter 15. Nothing else. Navigate: press or Space to advance | to go back

The smooth step Here's the problem with : imagine gradient descent trying to tune and inside . Nudge a little — the output usually doesn't change at all (it's still exactly 0 or exactly 1). The gradient is zero almost everywhere. Gradient descent is blind; there is no downhill to follow. We need a step with a slope — a function that goes from 0 to 1 but smoothly, so every nudge changes the output a little. What properties must this "smooth step" have? Quick Check — Sigmoid Saturation In Exercise 1.4, the sigmoid neuron "refused to learn" when given large input values. What caused this? A. Large values cause Python to crash with overflow errors B. The sigmoid function flattens to nearly 0 or 1 for large inputs — the gradient becomes almost zero, so gradient descent makes almost no progress C. Large values make the learning rate too high D. The sigmoid can only handle inputs between 0 and 1

fragments.text: Answer: B. Sigmoid's output is nearly flat for large positive or negative inputs — the derivative is practically zero, so gradient descent has no signal to follow. This is called saturation .

Quick Check — Why Multiple Neurons? A single sigmoid neuron can fit a smooth S-shaped curve. Why do we need multiple neurons? A. Multiple neurons run faster on modern hardware B. A single S-curve can only capture one transition (e.g., "low to high"), but real problems often have multiple transitions or complex shapes that require combining several curves C. Python limits each neuron to 10 weights D. Multiple neurons are needed only for classification, not regression

fragments.text: Answer: B. One sigmoid gives you one smooth transition. Real data has kinks, bumps, and multiple boundaries — you need to combine several neurons to approximate those shapes.

The right activation: ReLU Look at the tax rule one more time: zero below a threshold, a straight ramp above it. There is an activation function that is that shape: Your challenge: Before looking at any formula, write a function that outputs 0 for negative inputs and the input itself for positive inputs. That's the shape you need. Write (use so it works on arrays). Then reuse your on the model [math] — same starting point, same settings, only the activation changed. The tests expect near-perfection: the network can now represent the true rule exactly (one solution: — but gradient descent may find an equivalent scaling, e.g. ). The reveal: ReLU — the rectified linear unit — is the default activation of modern deep learning, powering nearly every large model. Sigmoid saturates at both ends (you met that plateau in Exercise 1.4); ReLU never saturates on the positive side, and stacks of ReLU neurons build arbitrary piecewise-linear shapes — kinks upon kinks, like the one you just fit with a single neuron. Quick Check — ReLU Advantage ReLU (max(0, z)) is simpler than sigmoid. What is its main practical advantage for training neural networks? A. ReLU outputs larger numbers, making predictions more accurate B. ReLU's gradient is either 0 or 1 — it never becomes a tiny fraction like sigmoid's, so gradient descent doesn't slow down for large inputs C. ReLU uses less memory than sigmoid D. ReLU can only be used in the output layer

fragments.text: Answer: B. For positive inputs, ReLU's derivative is always 1 — the gradient never vanishes. Sigmoid's derivative shrinks toward zero for large inputs (saturation), stalling learning.

Reflection Take a moment to think about what you built in this chapter: You started with a blunt step function and discovered it could not learn. What made sigmoid better, and what was its fatal weakness? Why did centering the inputs fix the "stuck at 0.6 error" problem? Could you explain the saturation trap to a friend? The tax problem needed a kink that no straight line can produce. You solved it three ways — pipeline, sigmoid net, ReLU net. Which was most satisfying, and why? A neural network is "just" a computation graph with tunable weights trained by gradient descent. Does that feel simpler or more complicated than you expected before this chapter?
